extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physics, biology, and philosophy of science (readers interested in foundations and conceptual clarity of physical laws)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for formulating, interpreting, and extending physical laws and conceptual models (laws of motion, mass, force, mechanistic explanations) and for their application to domains such as atoms, molecules, ether, and biology. Emphasizes operational definition, empirical range, and avoidance of metaphysical obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper measure/definition of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper measure of mass is found to be a ratio of mutual accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defining mass as a metaphysical 'quantity of matter' or as proportional to volume; define mass operationally via measurable ratios of mutual accelerations (see summary: 'The proper measure of mass is found to be a ratio of mutual accelerations').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat force as a measure, not a metaphysical cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is seen as a certain measure of motion, and not its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use force as an operational quantity (e.g., m × acceleration) rather than as an imperceptible metaphysical 'cause of change in motion'. This avoids metaphysical obscurities and keeps laws descriptive and operational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness and operational definitions in laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws must be explicit about terms such as 'body', 'force', 'rest', and the reference relative to which motion is defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State with respect to what motion is measured (reference bodies/frames), specify what 'body' refers to (prefer 'particle' when appropriate), and clarify what is meant by 'force applied' (what is the object whose motion changes and in what direction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit generalization to empirically verified ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that a law verified in one domain (e.g., particles of gross matter) holds universally for all corpuscles (atoms, molecules, ether-elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending laws beyond their observed range, ask whether the law still simplifies conceptions and whether it leaves recognized perceptual phases undescribed; be cautious and reserve judgment where empirical support is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and test superposition (modified action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the presence of additional bodies modifies the mutual actions (accelerations) between two corpuscles, i.e., whether 'modified action' occurs rather than simple superposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dogmatically accept the parallelogram/synthesis of forces as universally valid. Investigate whether component accelerations b and c are altered to b' and c' when superposed, since this affects the synthesis of complex motions from simple ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of parallelogram of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The parallelogram of forces follows when component actions are unmodified but may not be a true synthesis if modified action exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the parallelogram primarily to particles of gross 'matter'; its extension to atoms, molecules, or ether-elements requires continual reservation and empirical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider aspect/orientation effects in interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the 'aspect' (posture/orientation) of corpuscles influences absolute magnitudes of mutual accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that aspect likely matters for chemical atoms and molecules (and possibly prime-atoms depending on their structure), but seems negligible for gravitating bodies; include aspect effects in models for phenomena like crystallization and magnetization when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish bodies from particles in formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'particle' rather than the vague term 'body' when stating fundamental laws to avoid obscuring complex motions of composite bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite bodies can have internal motions (spin, changing axes) making 'body'-level statements ambiguous; laws intended as fundamental should be framed in terms of particles or explicitly specify which point or quantity (e.g., centre of mass) is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify relational character of motion and force
rubrics_metrics.description: All motion and force are relative; laws should indicate to what the motion and force are related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since motion is relative to other particles or frames, and force is a relative measure of motion, formulations should specify the surrounding circumstances or reference system that determine acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid projecting conceptual models as literal reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanism and conceptual machinery (ether, atoms, molecules) are modes of describing perceptual routines, not necessarily realities behind perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should assert the predictive/descriptive value of symbols without claiming metaphysical truth; projecting the model into perceptual reality invites dogmatism and metaphysical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for consistency with observed phenomena across scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether principles (e.g., Newton's laws, superposition) remain consistent when moving from macroscopic to microscopic/ether domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (e.g., absence of moon's influence on sun-earth mutual accelerations) to justify domain validity, but remain open to anomalies at molecular/atomic scales that may demand modified hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and limit use of physical terms in biology
rubrics_metrics.description: When biology borrows physical terms (matter, force, mechanism), their use must be re-defined or justified rather than assumed identical to physics' usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biologists should either use such terms figuratively (with re-definition) or explicitly adopt the physicist's meanings; physicists themselves must ensure clarity to avoid introducing metaphysical notions into biological reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conceptual simplification derived from underlying structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek to conceptualize simple underlying structures (e.g., ether constitution or gross matter structure) from which many mechanical laws may directly flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid describing one complex mechanism by another equally complex one; aim for models whose simple constitution explains multiple observed laws, enabling clearer and more fertile theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret laws as descriptive shorthand, not explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should be the description in conceptual shorthand of the routine of perceptual experience, not a statement of ultimate causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame theories and laws as tools for describing and predicting sequences of sense-impressions, and avoid asserting 'why' phenomena occur in metaphysical terms beyond empirical description.
